title: Three Ways to Redesign an AI-Vulnerable Assessment
author: Paul Matthews
summary: Paul Matthews offers a practical framework for redesigning classroom assessments that have become vulnerable to AI misuse, grounded in a personal cautionary story: a two-week capstone Independent Research Project he had coached students through for years, handed in complete by a student within the second lesson once generative AI made the take-home essay trivially offloadable. His governing principle is that any task a student can complete unsupervised on a computer must be assumed to be AI-accessible, and that assessment redesign should function as a "treasure hunt, not a witch hunt," oriented toward encouraging learning rather than prosecuting cheating. Matthews organizes his redesign options into three concrete pathways: substitution, replacing the vulnerable task entirely with formats like viva voce exams, Socratic dialogues, or practical demonstrations; addition, layering low-stakes authentication checks such as a fifteen-minute in-class reflection, a hand-drawn argument map, or a marking conference onto the existing task; and modification, restructuring the same core task's timeline into staged checkpoints (thesis, sources, outline, final draft) that give teachers regular visibility into a student's actual progress rather than a single high-stakes submission. He is explicit that these tweaks should be forecasted to students in advance rather than sprung on them after the fact, framing transparency as essential to preserving trust while still increasing the visibility teachers need into how student work is actually produced.
points: Grounds the entire framework in a specific cautionary anecdote: a two-week capstone research essay handed in complete after a single lesson once generative AI made the original take-home format trivially offloadable.

Frames assessment redesign explicitly as "a treasure hunt, not a witch hunt," positioning the goal as encouraging genuine learning and formation rather than catching or prosecuting AI-assisted cheating.

Distinguishes three concrete redesign pathways — substitution (swap the task format entirely, e.g. viva voce or practical demonstration), addition (layer on a low-stakes authentication check like an in-class reflection or marking conference), and modification (restructure the same task into staged checkpoints).

Notes that authentication additions don't prove AI misuse when absent, but do reveal whether the intended formation actually took place — "a $20 essay with a $2 reflection" is diagnostic even without being punitive.

Insists redesign changes must be forecast to students in the original assessment notice rather than introduced after the fact, arguing that springing new requirements on students after submission would erode trust.
quotes: Tasks that are easily offloadable, and stay with me here, will be easily offloaded by our students. In fact, the best way to ensure students miss out on crucial learning and formation is by operating under the assumption that our assessment tasks are still fit for purpose in an AI world.
I remember the first time I saw a student do a two-week task in a single day. I was gutted.
In an AI world, assessment should be a treasure hunt, not a witch hunt. It's about encouraging learning, not prosecuting cheating.
A $20 essay with a $2 reflection isn't proof that a student has outsourced to AI, but it does show us that the formation we had hoped for perhaps hasn't taken place.
And if there is nothing more than a few tumbleweeds for the first few steps and then a perfect, typo-free assessment is submitted, that's a good time to have a conversation with the learner.
Now that students can complete work in less time with less engagement than ever before, we need to be wise about how we assess student knowledge and skill.
